issues.legal_issue: A landlord cannot equitably set off rent and related charges accruing after delivery of possession against mesne profits arising from the landlord’s earlier wrongful possession when the demands arise from different transactions.
material_facts: The patnidars obtained possession and were awarded mesne profits for the period during which the landlord had wrongfully held the lands.
The landlord sought to deduct rent, revenue and cesses accruing after delivery of possession from the mesne profits payable under the decree.
The later rent demand arose from the landlord-tenant relationship after possession had been delivered, whereas the mesne profits demand arose from the landlord’s earlier wrongful possession.
The landlord could have pursued recovery of the later amounts by separate legal proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The landlord was not entitled to equitable set-off for amounts accruing after delivery of possession; the later demands had to be pursued separately.
issues.legal_principle: An equitable set-off is unavailable where the cross-demands do not arise out of the same transaction. Mesne profits for wrongful possession and rent or related obligations arising later from a landlord-tenant relationship have distinct causes of action. Equity does not assist a wrongdoer in using an earlier wrongful withholding to recover amounts that could have been pursued through ordinary legal proceedings.

predicates.mesne_profits_setoff_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to set off a landlord’s demand against a decree for mesne profits arising from wrongful possession.
predicates.possession_delivered_before_later_claims: The landlord’s claimed rent or related obligations accrued after the other party had received possession.
predicates.claims_arise_from_distinct_transactions: The mesne profits demand arose from wrongful possession, while the opposing demand arose from a separate relationship or obligation.
predicates.later_claims_could_be_pursued_separately: The landlord could seek recovery of the later-accruing amounts through separate legal proceedings.

issues.definition: When a mesne-profits set-off dispute involves claims accruing after possession was delivered and the demands arise from distinct transactions or the later demand could be pursued separately, the later demand cannot be equitably set off.

issues.legal_issue: Future interest on a mesne-profits decree may be reduced where the claimant delayed seeking ascertainment and the opposing party is not entitled to the asserted equitable set-off.
material_facts: The claimant did not seek an inquiry into the mesne profits for about twelve years.
The court rejected the landlord’s claim for equitable set-off for the period after delivery of possession.
The lower appellate court had allowed future interest at a higher rate in connection with its allowance of that set-off.
issues.conclusion: The future interest on the mesne-profits awards was reduced to four per cent rather than six per cent.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed future interest in light of the circumstances, including the claimant’s delay in seeking ascertainment of mesne profits and the rejection of the equitable set-off that had supported the higher rate.

predicates.mesne_profits_interest_dispute: The proceeding concerns future interest on a decree awarding mesne profits.
predicates.claimant_delayed_seeking_ascertainment: The claimant waited a substantial period before seeking an inquiry to determine the mesne profits.
predicates.equitable_setoff_rejected: The court rejected the opposing party’s claim to equitably set off its demand against the mesne profits.

issues.definition: In a dispute over future interest on mesne profits, delay by the claimant in seeking ascertainment, together with rejection of the asserted equitable set-off, results in an award at a reduced rate.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to the method for calculating additional rent may be rejected when raised only at a late appellate stage and unsupported by evidence needed to establish the proposed alternative.
material_facts: The landlord challenged the established method for calculating additional rent for the first time at the hearing before the court.
The challenge had not been included in the grounds of appeal or in the additional grounds previously presented.
The landlord offered no evidence showing the proportion the original rent bore to revenue and cesses.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to entertain the late challenge and held that the proposed alternative calculation had no substance in the absence of supporting evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A new appellate ground need not be entertained when raised only at a late stage without valid grounds for doing so. A proposed alternative method of calculating rent also lacks substance when the evidence necessary to support it is absent. The court referred to the method in Radhacharan v. Maharaja Ranjit Singh when addressing the challenge to the established calculation.

predicates.appellate_rent_calculation_challenge: The proceeding includes an appellate challenge to the method used to calculate rent.
predicates.new_ground_raised_late: The party first raised the challenge at a late stage rather than including it in the earlier appellate grounds.
predicates.supporting_evidence_absent: The party did not provide evidence needed to support the proposed alternative calculation.

issues.definition: An appellate challenge to a rent calculation is rejected when it is raised late and lacks the evidence needed to support the proposed alternative.
